El Salvador rushes some 1,000 troops to Haiti after gang ambush, source says

Reuters

28 October, 2026 06:00 am IST

Follow Us :

By Sarah Morland Oct 27 (Reuters) – El Salvador has sent about 1,000 troops to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed security mission went missing in a gang ambush on the outskirts of the capital on October 18, a security official in Haiti told Reuters on Tuesday.

The troops’ arrival aboard flights in recent days dramatically expands the Central American nation’s role in Haiti’s long-standing gang conflict. Yet it remains unclear who will command the new Salvadoran contingent, how long it will stay in Haiti or whether more forces will follow.

Neither the Haitian nor Salvadoran government immediately responded to requests for comment. The official in Haiti spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the security situation.

Show Full Article

The deployment comes as the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force has reached about 2,000 personnel, just over a third of its planned strength a year into its mandate, with little improvement in Haiti’s security.

Armed gangs in Haiti have meanwhile expanded their influence over the capital and surrounding regions through extortion and brutal attacks that have displaced nearly 1.5 million people.

Haiti’s leaders have sought international security support since 2022, despite the country’s fraught history of foreign intervention. Gangs’ influence grew rapidly after the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise, deepening an insecurity crisis that has caused authorities to repeatedly delay elections.

Pierre Esperance, head of Haiti’s National Human Rights Defense Network, welcomed the unusually rapid Salvadoran deployment and said he hoped it would help stop gangs from terrorizing civilians. But he warned that any operation must avoid harming residents trapped in gang-held neighborhoods.

“Not everybody living in gang-controlled areas are gangsters,” he said.

President Nayib Bukele last week announced a military operation to recover the missing Salvadorans, who remain unaccounted for since jumping from a burning vehicle during the ambush. He has not said how many troops would be sent.

The US provided C-130 transport aircraft to help move Salvadoran troops to Haiti, a US military official said.

Additional commercial and military flights between San Salvador and Port-au-Prince were visible on flight-tracking site Flightradar24 and were also reported by the Miami Herald.

A photo posted on X on Tuesday by a lawmaker from Bukele’s ruling party showed a plane carrying uniformed soldiers, some taking selfies.

NO CLAIM OF RESPONSIBILITY

Bukele has built strong domestic support through a hardline anti-crime campaign that several right-wing governments in the Americas have sought to emulate. Human rights groups however warn that the crackdown has come at the cost of due process and has been linked to hundreds of deaths in custody.

Bukele said the missing Salvadorans were air force technicians, returning to base from a market, and that he believed they were being held hostage by criminal groups.

No Haitian gang has claimed responsibility for the ambush. Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, has released videos denying that his group is holding the Salvadorans or was involved in the attack.

Before the ambush, El Salvador had deployed at least 124 personnel to the force. Bukele said they were pilots and technicians sent to evacuate wounded personnel, not combatants.

Alongside the international mission, Haiti’s government has also hired a private military company run by Blackwater founder Erik Prince – an ally of US President Donald Trump – which has since 2025 carried out controversial anti-gang drone operations.

Luis Contreras, a Salvadoran security and organized crime analyst, said he expected that at least some of the new troops would operate outside the UN-backed mission’s chain of command and could coordinate with Prince’s firm.

“The UN has lacked the political will to resolve the issue of the gangs in Haiti,” he said. “Once the whereabouts of the four members have been established, they will have to assess whether to engage in a direct and protracted confrontation.”

(Reporting by Sarah Morland in Mexico City, Gerardo Arbaiza in San Salvador and Harold Isaac in Port-au-Prince; Editing by Daina Beth Solomon, Bill Berkrot and Jonathan Spicer )

Hegseth likely to face questions on US role in Indo-Pacific at ASEAN summit

Reuters

28 October, 2026 05:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Karen Lema MANILA, Oct 28 (Reuters) – US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is likely to face questions about Washington’s commitment to the Indo-Pacific region when he meets Southeast Asian counterparts in the Philippines on Wednesday.

As the Iran war strains US military readiness and tension rises with China, the Pentagon said Hegseth’s attendance at the gathering in the Philippine province of Cebu would reaffirm Washington’s commitment to “peace through strength” in the Pacific.

Analysts said Southeast Asian nations could use meetings with Hegseth on the sidelines to seek clarity about the endgame in Iran, US expectations from allies and partners, and how the conflict’s demands square with commitments to the Indo-Pacific.

Show Full Article

“They will want to seek answers from the United States regarding certainty towards alliances and partnerships,” said Collin Koh, a security scholar at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

“And of course, the bigger elephant in the room is how does that juxtapose with US commitment to the Indo-Pacific or Western Pacific theatre.”

ECONOMIES GRAPPLING WITH IRAN WAR IMPACT

Southeast Asian economies are grappling with the effects of Iran war, while tension between host the Philippines and Beijing add another source of friction to a forum meant to promote dialogue and practical cooperation on security.

The Iran war, launched by US and Israeli strikes on February 28, has disrupted shipping and oil markets, exposing Southeast Asia’s vulnerability to imported-fuel shocks and pushing energy security higher on ASEAN’s agenda.

Greg Poling, director of the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative said Hegseth would get an opportunity at the gathering to tackle aspects regarding China, the disputed South China Sea and Washington’s commitments to its treaty allies.

“Most will want reassurance about U.S. commitment to the region, despite the political turmoil in Washington and the weakening of both U.S. capabilities and readiness by the war in Iran.”

The topic is critical for the Philippines, a US treaty ally whose ties with Beijing have soured amid repeated confrontations in the disputed South China Sea, Chinese sanctions and, more recently, a summoning of the Chinese ambassador.

China’s defence attaché in the Philippines will attend the meeting, its defence ministry said on Tuesday.

Days before the meeting, set for October 28 and 29, the Philippine military said it monitored and shadowed China’s Liaoning aircraft carrier group as it passed through waters off the southern Philippines toward the Celebes Sea.

Stronger signals were more likely to figure in talks among like-minded partners, added Poling.

Such partners include the Squad, a grouping of the United States, Japan, Australia and the Philippines, whose defence chiefs are set to meet on October 28.

EVENTUAL CHAIRMAN’S STATEMENT SEEN AS RESTRAINED

However, the eventual chairman’s statement was likely to be more restrained than talks behind closed doors and would employ familiar ASEAN language, said Koh.

Manila’s position as ASEAN chair while embroiled in a dispute with China was “particularly sensitive”, he added.

Poling said the Philippines had to balance “aspirational cooperation” on issues such as energy connectivity, the digital economy and coast guard cooperation against rising tension with China and stalled progress on a South China Sea code of conduct.

“For the Philippines, the whole ASEAN chair year has been a difficult balance,” added Poling, who is also a fellow with the Southeast Asia Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

“I’d expect tactical cooperation on the ADMM workstreams … but no strategic alignment on the South China Sea or other thorny issues,” he said, referring to the bloc’s effort to tackle issues such as maritime security and counter-terrorism.

(Reporting by Karen Lema; Editing by Clarence Fernandez)
